```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.5)
library(nlmixr2lib)
library(rxode2)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
```

# Model and source

Al-Huniti 2017 used the phase II study 07-IN-NX003 of naloxegol, a peripherally
acting mu-opioid receptor antagonist, to choose the doses for the phase III
programme. Two models were fitted jointly in NONMEM 7.2 (Laplace):

* a **longitudinal mixed-effects logistic regression** for the probability that
  a treatment week is a *responder week* (at least 3 spontaneous bowel movements
  (SBMs) and at least 1 SBM more than baseline), linear in the daily dose on the
  logit scale, with a random effect on the intercept and no time trend:
  `logit(P) = E0 + alpha * Dose + eta`;
* a **Weibull time-to-dropout model** parameterised by its median, which falls
  linearly with the daily dose: `median = B + beta * Dose`.

Both are in the single model file `AlHuniti_2017_naloxegol`, which outputs
`prob_sbm_response` (the weekly response probability) and `sur` (the
probability of still being in the study). There is no pharmacokinetic layer:
the nominal once-daily dose `DOSE` (mg) is the exposure metric.

* Citation: `r rxode2::rxode(readModelDb("AlHuniti_2017_naloxegol"))$reference`
* Article: <https://doi.org/10.1002/psp4.12229>

```{r load-model}
mod <- readModelDb("AlHuniti_2017_naloxegol")
ui <- rxode2::rxode(mod)
theta <- ui$theta
omega_e0 <- ui$omega["etalogite0", "etalogite0"]
theta[c("logite0", "e_dose_logit", "ltmed_drop", "e_dose_tmed_drop", "lalfa_drop")]
omega_e0
```

# Population

The analysis used the modified intention-to-treat population of the phase II
study: 185 adults with opioid-induced constipation taking opioids for chronic
noncancer pain (mean age 49.7 years, 62.2% women, 86.5% White and 11.4% Black,
body weight 50.2-182.1 kg). After a 1-week single-blind placebo run-in, three
sequential cohorts were each randomized 1:1 to placebo or naloxegol 5, 25 or
50 mg once daily for 4 weeks (Table 1: 95 placebo, 31 at 5 mg, 29 at 25 mg,
30 at 50 mg). A planned 100 mg cohort was not run. The same facts are in
`population` of the model metadata.

# Source trace

| Quantity | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Response model `logit(P) = E0 + alpha * Dose + eta` | -- | Methods, Model development (first equation) |
| Weibull density `p(t) = ln2 * gamma / t~ * (t / t~)^(gamma - 1) * exp(-ln2 * (t / t~)^gamma)` | -- | Methods, Model development (second equation) |
| Median time to dropout `t~ = B + beta * Dose` | -- | Methods, Model development (third equation) |
| `logite0` (E0) | -0.51 | Table 2 |
| `e_dose_logit` (alpha) | 0.061 per mg | Table 2 |
| `ltmed_drop` (B) | log(110 days) | Table 2 |
| `e_dose_tmed_drop` (beta) | -1.2 days per mg | Table 2 |
| `lalfa_drop` (gamma) | log(1.4) | Table 2 |
| `etalogite0` (variance of E0) | 2.6 | Table 2 |
| `addSd_prob_sbm_response`, `addSd_sur` | 0.001, fixed | not from the source (placeholders) |
| Response rates and dropout rates by dose | -- | Table 3, Figure 2 |
| Weekly fraction of responders by dose | -- | Figure 1 |
| Mean difference from placebo in responder proportion | -- | Figure 3 |

# Typical-value checks against the Results text

The Results state that the probability of response on placebo in any week is
0.38, that the odds ratio of response is about 1.8 per 10 mg, and that the
median time to dropout on placebo is 110 days and falls by about 12 days per
10 mg. The model is evaluated with its random effect set to zero on a small
dose grid. The model has no time dimension in its response part, so `time` on
these rows only orders them.

```{r typical}
mod_typ <- rxode2::zeroRe(ui, "omega")
# Typical-value solves: rxode2 warns that a multi-subject solve has no omega,
# which is the intent here, so only that warning is muffled.
solve_typ <- function(events) {
  withCallingHandlers(
    as.data.frame(rxode2::rxSolve(mod_typ, events = events, returnType = "data.frame")),
    warning = function(w) {
      if (grepl("without 'omega'", conditionMessage(w), fixed = TRUE)) invokeRestart("muffleWarning")
    }
  )
}
doses <- c(0, 5, 10, 12.5, 25, 30, 37.5, 50)

typ_ev <- data.frame(
  id = 1L,
  time = 28,
  evid = 0L,
  amt = 0,
  DOSE = doses
) |>
  mutate(id = seq_along(DOSE))
typ <- solve_typ(typ_ev)
stopifnot(nrow(typ) == length(doses))
typ <- typ |>
  mutate(DOSE = doses) |>
  select(DOSE, prob_sbm_response, tmed_drop, sur)
knitr::kable(typ, digits = 3)

p0 <- typ$prob_sbm_response[typ$DOSE == 0]
p10 <- typ$prob_sbm_response[typ$DOSE == 10]
or10 <- (p10 / (1 - p10)) / (p0 / (1 - p0))
stopifnot(
  round(p0, 2) == 0.38, # 'Probability of response on placebo ... 0.38'
  round(or10, 1) == 1.8, # 'odds ratio ... about 1.8 for every 10 mg'
  abs(typ$tmed_drop[typ$DOSE == 0] - 110) < 1e-8, # 'median time to dropout on placebo is 110 days'
  abs(typ$tmed_drop[typ$DOSE == 0] - typ$tmed_drop[typ$DOSE == 10] - 12) < 1e-8 # '12 days for every 10 mg'
)
```

The survivor function must equal 0.5 at the median time, and the hazard must
be the derivative of the cumulative hazard. Both sides use the same parameters,
so the tolerances are numerical.

```{r survival-identities}
chk_ev <- data.frame(
  id = 1:3,
  time = c(110, 80, 50),
  evid = 0L,
  amt = 0,
  DOSE = c(0, 25, 50)
)
chk <- solve_typ(chk_ev)
stopifnot(all(abs(chk$sur - 0.5) < 1e-10))

h <- 1e-3 * 28
deriv_ev <- data.frame(
  id = rep(1:2, each = 3),
  time = rep(c(28 - h, 28, 28 + h), 2),
  evid = 0L,
  amt = 0,
  DOSE = rep(c(0, 50), each = 3)
)
d <- solve_typ(deriv_ev)
num_haz <- sapply(split(d, d$id), function(x) diff(x$cumhaz_drop[c(1, 3)]) / (2 * h))
mod_haz <- sapply(split(d, d$id), function(x) x$hazard_drop[2])
stopifnot(all(abs(num_haz / mod_haz - 1) < 1e-4))
```

# Weekly probability of response (Figure 1)

Figure 1 of the paper is a visual predictive check of the fraction of
responders per week. Its blue median line is the population-average weekly
response probability, which is the typical logit averaged over the random
effect of E0. That expectation is computed here by numerical integration over
`etalogite0`, using the model's own variance. In every panel the week-0 point
is the placebo run-in, so it sits at the placebo level.

```{r marginal}
marginal_p <- function(logit_typ, k_min = 1, n = 1) {
  integrate(
    function(e) {
      p <- plogis(logit_typ + e)
      pbinom(k_min - 1, n, p, lower.tail = FALSE) * dnorm(e, 0, sqrt(omega_e0))
    },
    -Inf, Inf
  )$value
}
typ <- typ |>
  mutate(
    logit_typ = qlogis(prob_sbm_response),
    p_week_marginal = vapply(logit_typ, marginal_p, numeric(1)),
    p_3of4 = vapply(logit_typ, marginal_p, numeric(1), k_min = 3, n = 4)
  )

fig1_median <- tibble(
  DOSE = c(0, 5, 25, 50),
  # Blue median line of Figure 1 at weeks 1-4, read from the published
  # figure by the maintainers (precision about 0.01).
  figure1 = c(0.41, 0.465, 0.665, 0.86)
) |>
  left_join(select(typ, DOSE, p_week_marginal), by = "DOSE")
knitr::kable(fig1_median, digits = 3)
stopifnot(all(abs(fig1_median$p_week_marginal - fig1_median$figure1) < 0.02))
```

The stochastic check below simulates 200 patients per arm with their random
effects, draws each week's response, and resamples virtual trials of the phase
II arm sizes to give the 95% prediction interval drawn in Figure 1.

```{r vpc}
rxode2::rxSetSeed(20171005)
set.seed(20171005) # weekly Bernoulli draws and trial resampling use R's generator
n_per_arm <- 200
vpc_doses <- c(0, 5, 25, 50)
vpc_ev <- expand.grid(
  sid = seq_len(n_per_arm),
  week = 0:4,
  arm = vpc_doses
) |>
  mutate(
    id = as.integer(factor(paste(arm, sid))),
    time = 7 * week,
    evid = 0L,
    amt = 0,
    # The run-in week is on placebo in every arm.
    DOSE = ifelse(week == 0, 0, arm)
  ) |>
  arrange(id, time) |>
  select(id, time, evid, amt, DOSE)
arm_of_id <- vpc_ev |>
  filter(time > 0) |>
  distinct(id, arm = DOSE)

vpc_sim <- as.data.frame(rxode2::rxSolve(ui, events = vpc_ev, returnType = "data.frame"))
stopifnot(nrow(vpc_sim) == nrow(vpc_ev))
vpc_sim <- vpc_sim |>
  left_join(arm_of_id, by = "id") |>
  mutate(week = time / 7)

arm_n <- c(`0` = 95, `5` = 31, `25` = 29, `50` = 30) # Table 1 arm sizes
n_trials <- 300
vpc_trials <- lapply(vpc_doses, function(a) {
  arm_sim <- filter(vpc_sim, arm == a)
  ids <- unique(arm_sim$id)
  lapply(seq_len(n_trials), function(r) {
    pick <- sample(ids, arm_n[[as.character(a)]], replace = TRUE)
    rows <- arm_sim[match(rep(pick, each = 5), arm_sim$id) + rep(0:4, length(pick)), ]
    rows |>
      mutate(resp = rbinom(n(), 1, prob_sbm_response)) |>
      group_by(week) |>
      summarise(frac = mean(resp), .groups = "drop") |>
      mutate(arm = a, trial = r)
  }) |>
    bind_rows()
}) |>
  bind_rows()

vpc_summary <- vpc_trials |>
  group_by(arm, week) |>
  summarise(
    median = median(frac),
    lo = quantile(frac, 0.025),
    hi = quantile(frac, 0.975),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(panel = factor(ifelse(arm == 0, "Placebo", paste(arm, "mg")),
    levels = c("Placebo", "5 mg", "25 mg", "50 mg")
  ))

ggplot(vpc_summary, aes(week)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = median), colour = "blue") +
  geom_line(aes(y = lo), colour = "red", linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_line(aes(y = hi), colour = "red", linetype = "dashed") +
  facet_wrap(~panel) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(x = "Time (week)", y = "Fraction of responders")
```

Replicates Figure 1 of Al-Huniti 2017 (simulated median and 95% prediction
interval; the observed points are not reproduced).

```{r vpc-check}
vpc_post <- vpc_summary |>
  filter(week > 0) |>
  group_by(arm) |>
  summarise(sim_median = median(median), .groups = "drop") |>
  left_join(fig1_median, by = c("arm" = "DOSE"))
knitr::kable(vpc_post, digits = 3)
# Centre of the stochastic simulation against the exact expectation; the
# Monte Carlo error of one 200-patient arm is about 0.03.
stopifnot(all(abs(vpc_post$sim_median - vpc_post$p_week_marginal) < 0.08))
```

# Response and dropout rates (Table 3 and Figure 2)

A patient is a responder when at least 3 of the 4 treatment weeks are responder
weeks, and a patient who drops out within the 4 weeks is a non-responder.
Because the random effect sits only on the response logit and the dropout
model has no random effect, the two are independent given the dose, so the
expected responder rate is the probability of staying in the study to day 28
times the population-average probability of at least 3 responder weeks out of 4.

```{r table3}
table3 <- tibble(
  DOSE = c(0, 12.5, 25, 30, 37.5, 50),
  paper_response = c(26.7, 40.0, 50.0, 56.7, 60.0, 63.3),
  paper_dropout = c(11.1, 13.3, 16.7, 20, 23.3, 33.3)
)
tab3 <- typ |>
  filter(DOSE %in% table3$DOSE) |>
  transmute(
    DOSE,
    model_response = 100 * sur * p_3of4,
    model_dropout = 100 * (1 - sur)
  ) |>
  left_join(table3, by = "DOSE")
tab3 |>
  select(DOSE, model_response, paper_response, model_dropout, paper_dropout) |>
  rename(
    "Dose (mg/day)" = DOSE,
    "Response rate, model (%)" = model_response,
    "Response rate, Table 3 median (%)" = paper_response,
    "Dropout rate, model (%)" = model_dropout,
    "Dropout rate, Table 3 median (%)" = paper_dropout
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 1)

stopifnot(
  all(abs(tab3$model_response - tab3$paper_response) < 3),
  all(diff(tab3$model_dropout) > 0)
)
```

The response rates agree with Table 3 to within 2 percentage points at every
dose. The model's dropout rates at day 28 are below the Table 3 medians by
`r round(min(tab3$paper_dropout - tab3$model_dropout), 1)` to
`r round(max(tab3$paper_dropout - tab3$model_dropout), 1)` percentage points,
the gap growing with dose. Table 3 does not say how its
dropout column was counted and its medians include parameter uncertainty and
sampling of small trials (the values fall on a grid of 1/30). The dropout
probabilities that are consistent with the response column are those of day 28:
at 50 mg a 33% dropout would cap the response rate at
`r round(100 * (1 - 0.333) * typ$p_3of4[typ$DOSE == 50], 1)`%, below the
63.3% Table 3 reports, whereas the day-28 model value gives
`r round(tab3$model_response[tab3$DOSE == 50], 1)`%.

```{r figure2, fig.height = 4}
fig2_obs <- tibble(DOSE = c(0, 5, 25, 50), observed = c(22, 39, 69, 67))
dose_grid <- seq(0, 50, by = 1)
grid_ev <- data.frame(id = seq_along(dose_grid), time = 28, evid = 0L, amt = 0, DOSE = dose_grid)
grid <- solve_typ(grid_ev) |>
  mutate(
    DOSE = dose_grid,
    p_3of4 = vapply(qlogis(prob_sbm_response), marginal_p, numeric(1), k_min = 3, n = 4),
    response = 100 * sur * p_3of4
  )
ggplot(grid, aes(DOSE, response)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point(data = table3, aes(y = paper_response), shape = 4, size = 3) +
  geom_point(data = fig2_obs, aes(y = observed), colour = "blue", size = 2) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 100)) +
  labs(
    x = "Dose (mg)", y = "Responders (%)",
    caption = "Line: model expectation. Crosses: Table 3 medians. Blue: observed phase II."
  )
```

Replicates the median curve of Figure 2 of Al-Huniti 2017.

## Stochastic trial check

The same rates from a simulation of 200 patients per dose, drawing each
patient's weekly responses and a dropout time:

```{r table3-stochastic}
rxode2::rxSetSeed(20171006)
set.seed(20171006)
sim_doses <- table3$DOSE
st_ev <- expand.grid(sid = seq_len(n_per_arm), week = 1:4, arm = sim_doses) |>
  mutate(
    id = as.integer(factor(paste(arm, sid))),
    time = 7 * week,
    evid = 0L,
    amt = 0,
    DOSE = arm
  ) |>
  arrange(id, time) |>
  select(id, time, evid, amt, DOSE)
st <- as.data.frame(rxode2::rxSolve(ui, events = st_ev, returnType = "data.frame"))
stopifnot(nrow(st) == nrow(st_ev))
st_subj <- st |>
  mutate(resp = rbinom(n(), 1, prob_sbm_response)) |>
  group_by(id) |>
  summarise(
    DOSE = first(DOSE),
    n_resp = sum(resp),
    sur28 = sur[time == 28],
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    dropout = runif(n()) > sur28,
    responder = n_resp >= 3 & !dropout
  )
st_rates <- st_subj |>
  group_by(DOSE) |>
  summarise(
    sim_response = 100 * mean(responder),
    sim_dropout = 100 * mean(dropout),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  left_join(select(tab3, DOSE, model_response, model_dropout), by = "DOSE")
knitr::kable(st_rates, digits = 1)
# One 200-patient arm has a binomial standard error of about 3.5 percentage
# points; the centre across the six arms is held tighter than any single arm.
stopifnot(
  abs(median(st_rates$sim_response - st_rates$model_response)) < 5,
  mean(abs(st_rates$sim_response - st_rates$model_response)) < 6
)
```

## Difference from placebo (Figure 3)

Figure 3 prints the mean, over simulated trials, of the difference in percent
responders between each dose and placebo: 12.5 at 12.5 mg, 25.1 at 25 mg and
34.3 at 37.5 mg (the Results text rounds the last two to 25% and 34%).

```{r figure3}
fig3 <- tibble(DOSE = c(12.5, 25, 37.5), paper_mean_diff = c(12.5, 25.1, 34.3)) |>
  left_join(select(tab3, DOSE, model_response), by = "DOSE") |>
  mutate(model_diff = model_response - tab3$model_response[tab3$DOSE == 0])
knitr::kable(select(fig3, DOSE, model_diff, paper_mean_diff), digits = 1)
stopifnot(all(abs(fig3$model_diff - fig3$paper_mean_diff) < 1.5))
```

The paper's percentages of trials exceeding a 10%, 15% or 18% difference depend
on the parameter uncertainty that was sampled for each trial; the covariance
matrix of the estimates is not published, so those percentages are not
reproduced.

# Comparison with the later phase III studies

The Discussion compares the 4-week predictions with the 12-week phase III
studies K4 and K5: observed response rates were 35% and 41% at 12.5 mg
(model 40%) and 44% and 40% at 25 mg (model 50%). The phase III responder
definition (9 of 12 weeks, and 3 of the last 4) is stricter and dropout
accumulates over 12 weeks, so lower phase III rates are expected; the model is
not intended to predict a 12-week endpoint directly.

# NCA

No PKNCA analysis is included: the model has no concentration output, and the
exposure metric is the nominal daily dose.

# Assumptions and deviations

* **Placeholder residual error.** The response likelihood is Bernoulli and the
  dropout likelihood is the Weibull event-time density, so neither has a
  residual error. `addSd_prob_sbm_response` and `addSd_sur` are fixed
  placeholders (0.001) that let nlmixr2 accept the two observation
  declarations; they are not from the source.
* **Median on the log scale.** B is stored as `ltmed_drop = log(110)` and
  back-transformed; the dose slope beta is added on the linear scale, exactly
  as printed. The linear median becomes zero at about 92 mg/day, so the model
  should not be used above the studied 50 mg/day.
* **Closed-form cumulative hazard.** `cumhaz_drop = ln2 * (t / median)^gamma`
  is exact when the dose is constant from the start of treatment, which is the
  design of the study. A dose that changes during treatment would need the
  hazard integrated instead.
* **Run-in week.** The response model has no time term; the placebo-level
  week-0 point of Figure 1 is reproduced by setting `DOSE = 0` on the run-in
  record.
* **Parameter uncertainty.** The paper's trial simulations sampled the
  parameters from their asymptotic multivariate normal distribution. Only the
  relative standard errors are published (no correlations), so the checks here
  use the point estimates.
* **Figure 1 values** were read from the published figure by the maintainers;
  they are used only as a check, never to set a parameter.
* **Table 3 dropout column.** See the discussion under Table 3: the response
  column is reproduced to within 2 percentage points, the dropout column is
  higher than the day-28 model probability by up to about 7 percentage points, and
  the paper does not give enough detail to say why.
* **Study size in Methods.** Methods describes 500 trials of 200 patients per
  dose group for the phase III prediction, while the Table 3 percentages fall
  on a grid of 1/30. The expected rates computed here do not depend on the
  trial size.
